content: The human hands, also known as manus (plural: manūs), are two highly intricate, prehensile, and multi-fingered structures located at the distal ends of the arms in humans and other primates. These hands serve as the primary organs for physically interacting with and manipulating the environment. They are capable of performing a wide range of motor tasks, from gross motor skills, such as wielding a club, to fine motor skills, such as threading a needle. The fingertips of the hands are densely packed with nerve endings, making them the richest source of tactile feedback in the human body. This dense innervation allows the sense of touch to be closely associated with the hands. Each hand is predominantly controlled by the opposite hemisphere of the brain, a phenomenon that contributes to handedness, or the preference for using one hand over the other for tasks like writing. This preference is a significant individual trait. What defines a hand? While many mammals and other animals possess grasping appendages, such as paws, claws, or talons, these are not scientifically classified as hands. The term hand is reserved for the terminal appendages of the forelimbs in primates, which are characterized by the presence of opposable thumbs. True hands are unique to the mammalian order of primates. Humans typically have two hands, attached to the arms, except in rare cases of polydactyly or polymelia. Some primates, such as apes and monkeys, are sometimes described as having four hands because their feet have long toes and opposable halluces (big toes), which resemble thumbs and allow their feet to function similarly to hands. Additionally, some apes have toes that are longer than human fingers. Anatomy of the human hand The human hand consists of a broad palm (metacarpus) with five digits and is connected to the forearm via the wrist joint (carpus). The back of the hand is formally referred to as the dorsum of the hand. Digits The hand has four fingers and one thumb. The fingers are primarily used for fine manipulation and can fold over the palm to grasp objects. The thumb, which is connected to the trapezium bone, is located on one side of the hand and is parallel to the arm. Unlike the other fingers, the thumb can rotate approximately 90° on a plane perpendicular to the palm, enabling a wide range of movements. This unique ability is due to the presence of opposable thumbs, which can be brought into opposition with the fingers through a muscle action known as opposition. This feature is a defining characteristic of true hands. Bones The human hand contains 27 bones. These include: 8 carpal bones in the wrist, arranged in two rows of four. The proximal row (from lateral to medial) consists of the scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, and pisiform bones. The distal row (from lateral to medial) includes the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate bones. 5 metacarpal bones in the palm, one for each digit. Each metacarpal has a head and a shaft. 14 phalanges (digital bones) in the fingers and thumb. Each finger has three phalanges: the proximal, middle, and distal phalanges. The thumb has only two phalanges (lacking a middle phalanx). Additionally, sesamoid bones, which are small ossified nodes embedded in tendons, are present around the palm at the bases of the digits. These bones provide extra leverage and reduce pressure on underlying tissues. The number of sesamoid bones varies between individuals. Articulations The joints of the human hand are more complex and delicate than those of comparable structures in other animals. This complexity allows humans to operate a wide variety of tools and devices. The hand can also form a fist, which is used in combat or as a gesture. The key articulations of the hand include: Interphalangeal joints (between the phalanges) Metacarpophalangeal joints (between the metacarpals and phalanges) Intercarpal joints (between the carpal bones) The wrist joint (which may also be considered part of the forearm) Muscles and tendons The movements of the human hand are facilitated by two groups of muscles: extrinsic and intrinsic. Extrinsic muscles: These include the long flexors and extensors, which are located in the forearm. The muscle bellies of these muscles are situated in the forearm, and their tendons extend into the hand to control movement. Intrinsic muscles: These include the thenar and hypothenar muscles (responsible for thumb and small finger movements, respectively), the interosseous muscles (located between the metacarpal bones, with four dorsal and three volar muscles), and the lumbrical muscles. The lumbrical muscles are unique because they originate from the deep flexor tendons rather than from bones and insert into the dorsal extensor hood mechanism. The fingers have two long flexor muscles located on the underside of the forearm. The deep flexor attaches to the distal phalanx, while the superficial flexor attaches to the middle phalanx. These muscles enable the bending of the fingers. The thumb has one long flexor and a short flexor within the thenar muscle group. The thumb also has additional muscles in the thenar group, such as the opponens and abductor muscles, which allow for opposition and grasping. The extensor muscles, located on the back of the forearm, are connected to the dorsum of the fingers in a more complex manner than the flexors. These tendons unite with the interosseous and lumbrical muscles to form the extensor hood mechanism, which straightens the digits. The thumb has two extensor muscles in the forearm, whose tendons form the anatomical snuffbox. The index and little fingers have additional extensors, which are used for specific movements like pointing. The extensor tendons are organized into six separate compartments in the wrist. Variation Some individuals may have more than the usual number of fingers or toes, a condition known as polydactyly. Others may have additional metacarpal bones, often due to genetic disorders such as Catel-Manzke syndrome. The average length of an adult male hand is 189 mm, while the average length of an adult female hand is 172 mm. The average hand breadth is 84 mm for males and 74 mm for females.
